title: TPS — Beginner
summary: A third-person kit in build order: an over-the-shoulder camera, movement, use, the magazine, replicated health, a slot, a squadmate patrol, and a save.

sections.title: Over-the-shoulder camera
sections.why: IA_Aim traces from the camera and sets Aiming. This is not the interact graph.
reading: A third-person camera sits behind the shoulder. Aiming pulls that camera in. The aim graph is not the interact graph: interact asks an actor to do something, and aim only records that the player is looking down the sights. IA_Aim is the shoulder button. Its Triggered pin starts a line trace. The trace begins at the camera, because a trace from the feet hits the ground and the crosshair lies. A hit sets Aiming true. The boom camera reads that bool and shortens its arm. Tick does not move the boom.

UE5 spring arms and camera components already interpolate. The graph's job is the bool, not a per-frame offset. The generated function is Graph_IA_Aim. It traces on the visibility channel and, inside if (bHit), assigns Aiming = true. There is no else in the sample, so a later release action has to set Aiming false. Leaving the bool true after the button comes up keeps the camera tight while the player is running.

The pawn's movement graph writes Speed separately. The camera reads the pawn. It does not write Speed, and movement does not write Aiming. A wall between the camera and the character is the spring arm's own probe. Stuffing that probe into this trace makes one query answer two questions and the aim target drifts off the crosshair.

Interaction will trace again when the player presses use. That second trace is correct: aim and use are different questions. The weapon will later read Aiming to tighten spread. Health does not. Save may store Aiming if a cinematic needs it. It is not the first value to pack.

The figure is the real Camera aim graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Aim is the shoulder button. The boom camera reads Aiming. The aim trace starts at the camera, not at the feet. A hit means we are aiming at a target. True pulls the camera in. The camera component reads this. Do not move the boom on Tick. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 10 is `FHitResult Hit_tpl_camera_trace; bool bHit_tpl_camera_trace = false; if (UWorld* World_tpl_camera_trace = GetW`. Line 13 is `Aiming = true; // node:tpl_camera_set`.

Across this track, keep IA_Aim, Camera trace, Aiming distinct. IA_Aim traces from the camera and sets Aiming. This is not the interact graph. IA_Aim starts the camera trace. The excerpt sets Aiming = true on a hit. Execute_Interact is a different graph.

sections.title: Third-person movement
sections.why: IA_Move writes Speed. The camera reads the pawn and does not write it.
reading: Third-person movement is the same speed contract as any pawn, seen from behind. IA_Move is the stick. The graph compares it with zero and writes Speed. The spring arm and the aim bool do not choose the speed. If they did, looking down the sights would slow the pawn inside the camera graph, and a designer tuning the boom would retune the gait.

The excerpt branches on IA_Move > 0.f. The true body is Speed = 600.f. The else is Speed = 200.f. Character movement reads Speed as the walk speed. Animation, even a simple blend space before GASP, reads the same number. Writing it on Tick stomps a crouch an ability set a moment earlier, and the third-person mesh pops between cycles.

The camera section's Aiming bool can scale Speed later, as a multiply after this write, owned by one function. Doing that multiply in both graphs writes the value twice. Interaction, the weapon, and the squadmate all follow the pawn this speed moves. They do not assign Speed. Save can store it. The input asset cannot.
A released stick must take the walk literal. If the false path is empty, the pawn sprints until something else writes Speed. That is the bug to look for in the else of the excerpt.

The figure is the real Movement graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Move is the axis. The character movement component consumes Speed. Zero axis means the stick is released. Greater than zero means the player is pushing move. A live axis takes the fast path. A released axis walks. Sprint speed. Walk speed. Write sprint speed. Write walk speed. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 9 is `Speed = 600.f; // node:tpl_movement_sprint`. Line 13 is `Speed = 200.f; // node:tpl_movement_walk`.

Across this track, keep IA_Move, Speed, Camera distinct. IA_Move writes Speed. The camera reads the pawn and does not write it. if ((IA_Move > 0.f)) sets Speed = 600.f, else Speed = 200.f. The camera does not write Speed.

sections.title: Third-person interaction
sections.why: Use traces from the camera and calls Interact. Aim only set a bool.
reading: Use, in third person, starts at IA_Interact. The trace should still come from the camera, along the crosshair, not from the pawn's chest. A chest trace hits the cover the camera can see past, and the prompt lights up on the wrong actor. The hit bool branches. The true path calls Interact through ProcessEvent. A door, a weapon on the ground, and a switch share that name.

The excerpt is Graph_IA_Interact. It traces, then if (bHit) looks up Interact on the hit actor. The else logs that there is nothing to use. That log is the miss. It is not a second trace. The aim graph already set Aiming. This graph does not write Aiming, or using a door would pull the camera in.

A cast to one door class fails the weapon on the ground. The function lookup is the interface. Overlap, used later by inventory, is a different question: something touched the capsule. Use is something the player pointed at.

The squadmate does not run this trace. Giving the companion the player's interact action makes the companion steal doors. Health does not trace. Save does not. One trace per press is the cost. A Tick trace, so the prompt can hover, is a separate cheaper query if you add it later, and it does not belong in this function.

The figure is the real Interact graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Interact fires when the player presses the interact key. Keep the key on the input action, not in this graph. A short line trace from the camera. Hit is true when something solid is in front of the player. Only talk to an actor when the trace hit. A miss should do nothing expensive. Call Interact through an interface. The door, the chest, and the switch can all answer. A The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 10 is `FHitResult Hit_tpl_interact_trace; bool bHit_tpl_interact_trace = false; if (UWorld* World_tpl_interact_trace `. Line 13 is `if (AActor* Target_tpl_interact_call = Cast<AActor>(Hit_tpl_interact_trace.GetActor())) { if (UFunction* Fn_tp`.

Across this track, keep IA_Interact, Line trace, ProcessEvent distinct. Use traces from the camera and calls Interact. Aim only set a bool. IA_Interact starts the trace. ProcessEvent looks up Interact. IA_Aim is the camera, not this graph.

sections.title: Third-person weapon
sections.why: IA_Reload checks the magazine and the reserve, then clamps.
reading: The third-person weapon carries a magazine the camera can see. Reload is still IA_Reload, not a tick and not the aim button. Magazine is the rounds in the gun. Reserve is the rounds on the body. MagSize is the cap. The excerpt branches on (Magazine < MagSize) && (Reserve > 0). Only then does it clamp the reserve into the gap: Needed = FMath::Clamp(Reserve, 0, (MagSize - Magazine)), add that to Magazine, and subtract it from Reserve.

That clamp is the whole safety. Without it a reload past a full magazine pulls rounds that do not fit. The else logs Cannot reload. Aiming, from the camera graph, may slow the reload animation. It does not change the arithmetic. Doing the arithmetic in the anim blueprint as well desyncs the visible mag and the count.

Health is not decremented here. A shot later calls damage. Inventory can fill Reserve from a stack, through the slot interface, and this graph consumes Reserve. Save stores both counts. The companion does not reload the player's magazine.
Spawning one actor per round, so the third-person mesh can show each bullet, replicates noise. The mesh reads Magazine and hides a bullet static mesh locally. The count is the state.

The figure is the real Tactical FPS: Ammo & Reload graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. IA_Reload is the key. The magazine and the reserve live on the weapon component, not in the widget. Rounds currently in the gun. Read this before any Set, because a later Get sees the new value. How many rounds the magazine holds when it is full. Reload only if the magazine is not already full. Rounds still in the pack. This is what a reload spends. Zero reserve means there The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 9 is `Needed = FMath::Clamp(Reserve, 0, (MagSize - Magazine)); // node:tpl_tactical-ammo_setneed`. Line 10 is `Magazine = (Magazine + Needed); // node:tpl_tactical-ammo_setmag`.

Across this track, keep IA_Reload, Magazine, Reserve, Clamp distinct. IA_Reload checks the magazine and the reserve, then clamps. IA_Reload starts it. Needed = FMath::Clamp(Reserve, 0, (MagSize - Magazine)). The mesh hides local bullets from Magazine.

assignment.model: IA_Reload starts it. Needed = FMath::Clamp(Reserve, 0, (MagSize - Magazine)). The mesh hides local bullets from Magazine.

sections.title: Third-person health
sections.why: Any Damage writes Health on the authority. OnRep updates the third-person hit reaction.
reading: Third-person health is a replicated float with a body the other players can see. Any Damage is the event. The excerpt tests HasAuthority in an empty block and then assigns Health = 90.f. The 90 is a sample literal. The empty block is the defect: a hit reaction on every client must not be what writes the float, or two players see two different bodies fall. Nest the assignment inside the authority check, and compute the value instead of typing 90.

OnRep_Health logs that health changed. On a third-person pawn that notify plays the flinch on the mesh everyone can see. It does not subtract again. The camera does not shake from this function. The local client can shake from the notify. The weapon calls the damage event. It does not assign Health.

The magazine, the aim bool, and the squadmate's patrol are unrelated floats. Save stores Health after the server writes it. A Tick that drains health, so the third-person mesh can bleed, ignores the event and bleeds while the player is standing in a menu.
A client that predicts the flinch is fine. A client that predicts the number is the snap you see when the server float arrives.

The figure is the real Replicated health graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Any Damage is the request. Authority decides. Has Authority keeps the change on the server. A stand-in for health after the hit. Set the replicated health. OnRep runs on the clients that hear the property. The UI listens. It does not decide the number. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 9 is `if (HasAuthority()) { /* authority */ } // node:tpl_replicated-health_auth`. Line 10 is `Health = 90.f; // node:tpl_replicated-health_set`.

Across this track, keep Any Damage, Has Authority, OnRep distinct. Any Damage writes Health on the authority. OnRep updates the third-person hit reaction. Put the write inside HasAuthority. OnRep plays the flinch and does not subtract.

sections.title: Third-person inventory
sections.why: Overlap calls AddToSlot. The use-trace does not count the stack.
reading: A third-person pickup touches the capsule. Overlap is the event, not the aim trace and not IA_Interact. The excerpt tests StackCount > 0.f, then ProcessEvent on AddToSlot of the other actor. The false path stores StackCount = 0.f. The test is a sample. A real slot also compares against the stack size on the item asset before it accepts more.

The visible backpack is a mesh on the pawn. It reads the count. It is not a replicated actor per item. The use trace can show a prompt when the camera looks at a pickup that has not overlapped yet. The prompt does not increment the count. If it did, looking at a pile would fill the bag.

The weapon's Reserve is what an ammo stack fills, by a call into the reload component after AddToSlot succeeds. Health items call the damage event with a heal. They do not write Health in this overlap. Save stores StackCount. The companion must not run the player's overlap, or the squadmate loots the bag.
A Tick that scans for nearby pickups repeats the physics overlap and still needs this interface at the end.

The figure is the real Inventory slot graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Overlap is the item touching the pawn. Read the stack the component already owns. Zero means the slot is empty. Greater asks if the stack is above zero. Branch before the interface call. Call the interface. Do not cast. The else path keeps the current count. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 12 is `if (AActor* Target_tpl_inventoryslot_call = Cast<AActor>(OtherActor)) { if (UFunction* Fn_tpl_inventoryslot_ca`. Line 16 is `StackCount = 0.f; // node:tpl_inventory-slot_store`.

Across this track, keep Overlap, StackCount, AddToSlot distinct. Overlap calls AddToSlot. The use-trace does not count the stack. Overlap calls AddToSlot when StackCount > 0. The aim and use traces only prompt.

sections.title: Squadmate patrol
sections.why: AdvancePatrol runs from a timer. The squadmate does not tick a path.
reading: The third-person squadmate walks a short route beside the player. Begin Play starts a timer that calls AdvancePatrol. The excerpt sets that timer for 1.f, not looping in this sample, so a finished route has to start the next timer on purpose rather than stacking timers. AdvancePatrol flips a bool and assigns GoingRight = true on the A path. The B path in the sample is empty, which means the return direction is the line you still owe the graph.

Tick that moves the companion every frame also moves it while the player is in a menu and pays a query the timer already scheduled. The route points are data. The timer only picks the next one. The companion does not run IA_Aim, IA_Interact, or the player's reload. Giving it those actions makes it face the player's camera and steal doors.

Health on the companion is its own component if it can be shot. It is not the player's Health float. Inventory overlap stays on the player. Save may store the companion's next point. It does not store the player's Aiming in the companion slot.
The flip-flop is the memory of which way the last step went. Resetting it on Tick loses the route.

The figure is the real AI patrol graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Play starts the patrol timer once. Set Timer by Function calls Advance Patrol. The timer calls this event. FlipFlop swaps direction each time. True means the next point is to the right. Store the direction. Do not replicate the mesh. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 8 is `if (UWorld* World = GetWorld()) { FTimerHandle Timer_tpl_aipatrol_timer; World->GetTimerManager().SetTimer(Tim`. Line 14 is `Flip_tpl_aipatrol_flip = !Flip_tpl_aipatrol_flip;`.

Across this track, keep Begin Play, AdvancePatrol, GoingRight distinct. AdvancePatrol runs from a timer. The squadmate does not tick a path. SetTimer calls AdvancePatrol. The A path sets GoingRight = true. Tick does not walk the route.

sections.title: Third-person save
sections.why: Begin Play loads the pawn, the mag, and the companion point.
reading: The third-person slot packs Health, Magazine, Reserve, StackCount, Aiming only if a mode needs the camera tight on load, and the companion's next route point. It does not pack the spring-arm mesh or the mapping context. Begin Play is the load, because the camera, the weapon, and the squadmate exist. The excerpt assigns SlotValue = 1.f after building a vector stand-in, and LoadSlot logs Loaded after a break stand-in.

A Tick write stores a reload that has not finished and a companion halfway between points with GoingRight already flipped. The player comes back to a route that skips a corner. Write the struct when the player asks, or on a slow autosave event, not on Tick.

The authority must have written Health before the pack, or the slot stores a client guess and the third-person body stands back up wrong. The camera boom length is derived from Aiming. Store the bool if you must. Do not store the boom transform.

Load runs after Begin Play has created the components. The constructor is too early. The companion timer starts after the loaded point is applied, or it steps from the default before the save arrives.

The figure is the real Save / load slot graph, with that preset's node positions and wires. Begin Play writes the slot once. Do not write it from Tick. The member written into the payload. Make Struct builds the save payload. Keep the member on the component. Load is its own event. It does not run during the save. Break Struct reads one member. A print stands in for the load UI. The C++ beside the figure is the compiler output for this same graph. Line 8 is `FVector Made_tpl_saveload_make = FVector::ZeroVector; Made_tpl_saveload_make.X = 1.f; Made_tpl_saveload_make.Y`. Line 9 is `SlotValue = 1.f; // node:tpl_save-load_store`.

Across this track, keep Begin Play, SlotValue, LoadSlot distinct. Begin Play loads the pawn, the mag, and the companion point. Begin Play loads. GoingRight, or the next route point, is packed. The boom transform is not.
